resources.string: Shows whether Adwarden is actively filtering and inspecting traffic.
Turn on protection to see live throughput
No blocks recorded yet. Turn on protection to start building history.
Start to filter and inspect on-device traffic
Allowed traffic is forwarded through the native core; blocked domains and apps are dropped.
Block an app on Wi-Fi and mobile independently, or opt it into HTTPS inspection (lock). Enforced while protection is on.
Turn on protection to watch traffic live
Turn it on to watch connections in real time. This does not change filtering.
Network-level rules apply on the VPN. Cosmetic and scriptlet rules need a browser and are ignored.
Apps\' own DoT/DoH is left untouched — not filtered, and not routed through the upstream server below.
Deny DoT/DoH so queries fall back to plaintext — filtered, then sent to the upstream server below.

Decrypt DoT/DoH and apply the blocklist to the queries inside; allowed ones still go to the app\'s own resolver, not the upstream server below. Needs the Adwarden CA installed; flows we can\'t decrypt (pinned apps, Private DNS strict, QUIC) are blocked instead.

Where Adwarden forwards the allowed plaintext queries apps send it. Plain sends cleartext to an IP (blank = the default 1.1.1.1); DoT and DoH encrypt lookups to a named resolver — pick a preset or enter your own. A misconfigured or unreachable encrypted resolver blocks DNS rather than falling back to cleartext.

The upstream server and blocklist only apply to the queries apps send Adwarden in plaintext. Apps that use their own DoT/DoH bypass both — set Encrypted DNS to Block to force them onto plaintext. Filter still blocklist-checks their DNS, but forwards allowed queries to the app\'s own resolver, not the upstream server.
Filtering encrypted DNS requires the Adwarden CA. Android Private DNS in strict mode validates the system trust store and can\'t be decrypted, so it is blocked rather than filtered.
Master switch. Choose which apps to inspect on the Apps tab; nothing is intercepted until you do. Install the CA first. Applies on next connection.
Trust the root certificate so decryption can work.
Without root, Android only lets us decrypt apps that trust user certificates (e.g. Chrome). Blocking, logging and PCAP still work for every app.
Inject CSS to hide ad slots and boxes that survive network blocking, on inspected apps.
Advanced: injects JavaScript into pages to defuse anti-adblock and ad scripts. Downloads a scriptlet pack.
Cosmetic filtering only works on apps you\'ve enabled HTTPS inspection for (with the Adwarden CA installed) — Chrome and Firefox. It never touches other apps.
Plaintext connection to the proxy, which tunnels traffic with CONNECT. Use this for most proxies — including lists labelled \"HTTPS\", whose entries are usually plaintext HTTP proxies.

Connects to the proxy itself over TLS — only for proxies that terminate TLS (uncommon), with a publicly-trusted certificate matching the host. Most \"HTTPS\" proxy lists are actually plaintext: use HTTP for those.
SOCKS5 with optional login. Carries DNS and other UDP (e.g. QUIC) too; if the proxy doesn\'t support UDP, DNS falls back to TCP automatically.

Off by default. When off, DNS goes directly to the resolver (using the transport above — plain, DoT or DoH), even while a proxy carries your other traffic. When on, DNS rides the proxy instead: a SOCKS5 proxy carries it (falling back to TCP if it refuses UDP), an HTTP/HTTPS proxy over TCP (CONNECT to the resolver\'s port, which some refuse). Routing through the proxy is always plain DNS — a DoT/DoH upstream is sent as plaintext to port 53 and loses its encryption on that leg.

Allowed TCP connections are sent through the proxy; if it can\'t be reached, the connection is blocked rather than leaking around it. Non-DNS UDP (e.g. QUIC) goes through a SOCKS5 proxy, or is dropped for an HTTP/HTTPS proxy so apps fall back to TCP. DNS follows the switch above, independent of the proxy. Changing the host/type/port reconnects the VPN.
Open Android\'s VPN settings to keep Adwarden always connected, and optionally block traffic while it\'s off (lockdown).
Add the Adwarden tile from the Quick Settings edit panel to toggle protection without opening the app.
Filtering, the per-app firewall and HTTPS inspection all run in a native core on your phone — no traffic is sent to any server.

Since Android 7, apps only trust user-installed CAs if they opt in. Browsers like Chrome and Firefox do; many apps pin their certificates and stay opaque. Blocking, logging and PCAP keep working for every app — only full HTTPS decode is limited to the cooperating subset.

1. Tap Install certificate below.
2. The system will ask what to install — choose "CA certificate".
3. Confirm the security warning to trust the Adwarden CA.
If the picker doesn't appear, use Export .pem, then Settings ▸ Security & privacy ▸ More security ▸ Encryption & credentials ▸ Install a certificate ▸ CA certificate, and pick the exported file.

1. Tap Install certificate below and choose \"CA certificate\".\n2. Confirm the security warning.\nOtherwise Export .pem and install it via Settings ▸ Security ▸ Encryption & credentials ▸ Install a certificate ▸ CA certificate.
Tap Install certificate and choose \"CA certificate\", or Export .pem and install it from Settings ▸ Security ▸ Install from storage.
Block ads and trackers, run a per-app firewall, and inspect every connection — no root required.
Subscribe to AdGuard and EasyList rule sets, or write your own.
Cut off any app on Wi-Fi or mobile data independently.
Watch connections in real time and export PCAP for analysis.
Adwarden filters and inspects traffic through a local, on-device VPN. There is no remote server — the tunnel never leaves your phone. Android shows a one-time consent prompt for this.
While protection runs, Android keeps a permanent notification so you always know Adwarden is active. Allow it to keep that indicator visible.
Turn on protection from the dashboard whenever you\'re ready. To decrypt HTTPS for inspection later, install the Adwarden CA — it\'s optional and off by default.
